before: MMI affects when you can settle your case, how your permanent impairment is rated, whether your workers' comp benefits change from temporary to permanent, and ultimately how much money you recover. Understanding MMI — and knowing what to do if you disagree with the determination — is essential to protecting the full value of your claim. For background on how disability determinations work in legal contexts, the Cornell Law Institute's workers' compensation overview provides useful foundational context.

For background on how disability determinations work in legal contexts, the Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute overview of workers' compensation provides useful foundational context.

before: Insurance companies and workers' compensation carriers frequently request an independent medical examination (IME) to obtain a second opinion on MMI. Despite the name, IME physicians are selected and paid by the insurance company, which creates an inherent incentive to find that MMI has been reached sooner rather than later — since an earlier MMI determination allows the insurer to reduce or terminate benefits.
after: Insurance companies and workers' compensation carriers frequently request an independent medical examination (IME) to obtain a second opinion on MMI. Despite the name, IME physicians are selected and paid by the insurance company, which creates an inherent incentive to find that MMI has been reached sooner rather than later — since an earlier MMI determination helps the insurer argue for reducing or ending benefits.

before:
• Georgia: The employer or insurer has the right to select the authorized treating physician (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201). This physician's MMI determination is presumptively valid unless challenged.
  • South Carolina: The employer similarly directs initial medical care, though the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission may authorize a change of physician in certain circumstances (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).
after:
• Georgia: The employer posts a panel of at least six physicians and you choose your authorized treating physician from it; you may switch once within the panel without Board approval (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-201). That physician's MMI opinion carries the most weight before the State Board of Workers' Compensation unless you challenge it with other medical evidence.
  • South Carolina: The employer chooses the treating doctor outright, though the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission may authorize a change of physician in certain circumstances (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).

before:
• Georgia TTD: Paid at two-thirds of your average weekly wage, subject to a maximum weekly benefit set annually by the State Board of Workers' Compensation (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261). TTD benefits are available for up to 400 weeks.
  • South Carolina TTD: Paid at 66 2/3% of your average weekly wage, subject to a maximum set by the South Carolina Workers' Compensation Commission (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). TTD benefits continue until you return to work or reach MMI.
after:
• Georgia TTD: Paid at two-thirds of your average weekly wage, capped by statute at $800 per week for injuries on or after July 1, 2023 (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-261). TTD benefits are available for up to 400 weeks, except for catastrophic injuries.
  • South Carolina TTD: Paid at 66 2/3% of your average weekly wage, subject to a maximum tied to the state average weekly wage — $1,189.94 per week for injuries on or after January 1, 2026 (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). TTD is capped at 500 weeks and normally ends when you return to work or are released to full duty; after MMI the insurer must ask the Commission for permission to stop it (S.C. Code § 42-9-260).

before:
Once you reach MMI, if you have a permanent impairment, your benefits transition from temporary to permanent. This is where the impairment rating becomes critical:

  • Permanent partial disability (PPD): If you have a permanent impairment but can still work in some capacity, you may receive PPD benefits based on your impairment rating and the body part affected.
  • Permanent total disability (PTD): In rare cases involving catastrophic injuries, you may be found permanently and totally disabled, entitling you to benefits for the rest of your life.

The transition from TTD to PPD often results in a significant reduction in weekly benefit payments. Insurers have a financial incentive to push for an early MMI determination, which is why having an attorney review the medical evidence and challenge premature MMI conclusions is essential.

Once you reach MMI and your temporary benefits end, if you have a permanent impairment your benefits shift from temporary to permanent — in Georgia PPD is not paid while TTD or TPD is owed (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263), and in South Carolina the insurer needs the Commission's permission to stop TTD after MMI. This is where the impairment rating becomes critical:

  • Permanent partial disability (PPD): If you have a permanent impairment but can still work in some capacity, you may receive PPD benefits based on your impairment rating and the body part affected.
  • Permanent total disability (PTD): In rare cases involving catastrophic injuries, you may be found permanently and totally disabled, entitling you to benefits beyond the ordinary caps — for life in South Carolina paraplegia, quadriplegia and brain-injury cases, and in Georgia for as long as the catastrophic disability continues.

The transition from TTD to PPD usually means a large reduction in total benefits: PPD is paid at the same weekly rate but only for a fixed number of weeks set by the impairment rating and the schedule. Insurers have a financial incentive to push for an early MMI determination, which is why having an attorney review the medical evidence and challenge premature MMI conclusions is essential.

before: Most physicians use the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment as the standard reference for calculating impairment ratings. The edition used matters — Georgia workers' compensation generally references the AMA Guides, and South Carolina does as well, though the specific edition and application may vary.
after: Most physicians use the AMA Guides to the Evaluation of Permanent Impairment as the standard reference for calculating impairment ratings. The edition used matters — Georgia workers' compensation requires ratings under the fifth edition (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263); South Carolina mandates no edition, and its Commission accepts the AMA Guides or any other accepted medical authority.

before: When an insurance company requests an IME, they select a physician from a roster of doctors who regularly perform evaluations for insurers. These physicians understand that their continued referral business depends on producing results the insurer finds useful. While not every IME doctor is biased, the structural incentive to minimize injuries and declare early MMI is real and well-documented.

before:
• Cursory examinations: IME physicians may spend only 15-20 minutes examining you, compared to the hours your treating physician has invested over months of care.
  • Cherry-picking records: The IME doctor may focus selectively on records that support a favorable-to-insurer conclusion while ignoring contrary evidence.
  • Premature MMI conclusions: The IME physician may declare MMI earlier than your treating doctor, allowing the insurer to terminate temporary benefits sooner.
  • Lower impairment ratings: IME doctors frequently assign lower impairment ratings than treating physicians, reducing the permanent disability benefits or settlement value.

before: Maximum medical improvement means your condition has stabilised, not that you are healed. Why MMI is the turning point in an injury claim.
after: Maximum medical improvement means your condition has stabilized, not that you are healed. Why MMI is the turning point in an injury claim.

before: Maximum medical improvement (MMI) is when your condition stabilizes — not when you are fully healed. In Georgia, MMI ends TTD and triggers PPD based on impairment rating (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263); catastrophic injuries get lifetime benefits (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1). In South Carolina, MMI triggers PPD within the 500-week cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10, § 42-9-30). Medical benefits continue after MMI in both states. Do not settle a PI case before reaching MMI — and challenge premature determinations.
after: Maximum medical improvement (MMI) is when your condition stabilizes — not when you are fully healed. In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned; PPD (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD ends, and MMI alone does not end TTD; catastrophic injuries are not subject to the 400-week caps (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1). In South Carolina, MMI triggers PPD within the 500-week cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10, § 42-9-30). Medical benefits continue after MMI in both states, subject to Georgia's 400-week limit for non-catastrophic injuries. Do not settle a PI case before reaching MMI — and challenge premature determinations.

before: In Georgia, reaching MMI typically ends temporary total disability (TTD) benefits and triggers a transition to permanent partial disability (PPD) benefits based on your impairment rating (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263). For catastrophic injuries, lifetime benefits may continue under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200.1. Medical benefits continue regardless of MMI.
after: In Georgia, MMI is when your impairment rating is assigned. It does not by itself end temporary total disability (TTD) — TTD generally continues until you return to work, are released to full duty, or hit the 400-week cap — and permanent partial disability (PPD) (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-263) is paid once TTD or TPD stops. For catastrophic injuries the 400-week caps do not apply (O.C.G.A. §§ 34-9-261, 34-9-200.1). Medical benefits continue after MMI, for up to 400 weeks in non-catastrophic cases.

before: In South Carolina, MMI similarly ends TTD and triggers PPD benefits based on impairment rating and loss of earning capacity (S.C. Code § 42-9-30). The 500-week overall benefit cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10) continues to apply. Medical benefits for the work injury continue after MMI with no time limit.
after: In South Carolina, MMI lets the insurer ask the Commission to stop TTD (S.C. Code § 42-9-260) and starts the permanent-disability phase — scheduled PPD by impairment rating (§ 42-9-30) or wage-loss benefits (§ 42-9-20). The 500-week overall benefit cap (S.C. Code § 42-9-10) continues to apply. Medical benefits for the work injury can continue after MMI as long as the Commission finds treatment will lessen your disability — but they end one year after a Form 16 settlement is paid out or after a year without authorized treatment, so keep treating (S.C. Code § 42-15-60).

before: You can (1) request a second opinion from an independent physician, (2) have your attorney challenge the determination through the workers' comp board or in court, (3) provide additional medical evidence showing you have not yet stabilized, or (4) request that the court appoint an independent medical examiner. Do not accept a premature MMI without legal advice.
after: You can (1) request a second opinion from an independent physician, (2) have your attorney request a hearing — Form WC-14 with Georgia's State Board or Form 50 with South Carolina's Commission, (3) provide additional medical evidence showing you have not yet stabilized, or (4) in Georgia, use your one-time independent examination at the insurer's expense within 120 days of your first income-benefit check (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-202(e)); in South Carolina, ask the Commission to order an examination (S.C. Code § 42-15-80). Do not accept a premature MMI without legal advice.
